proof:
# A shared enclosing simplex imposes an actual facet-volume budget

These are geometric necessary conditions in the normalized zero-endpoint
regime of `candidate 568f7cf028ec23b6`.
They do not resolve OC, and their geometric sharpness does not assert
that every extremizer is a genuine mixed-depth critical configuration.

## 1. A dimension-independent pyramid inequality

Let T be a d-simplex, d>=2, with facets G_i and affine barycentric
coordinates lambda_i, where G_i={lambda_i=0}. Let B be a full-dimensional
compact convex body contained in T. Put F_i=B intersect G_i and

    f_i=H_(d-1)(F_i)/H_(d-1)(G_i),  0<=f_i<=1.

For every p in B,

    |B|/|T| >= sum_i f_i lambda_i(p).                 (1)

Indeed each pyramid conv(p,F_i) is contained in B. If p is interior
to T, the larger pyramids conv(p,G_i) partition T up to sets of zero
d-volume, so the smaller pyramids have disjoint interiors. Their
relative volumes are f_i lambda_i(p): the base-area ratio is f_i and
the height from p to G_i, divided by the corresponding height from
the opposite vertex, is lambda_i(p). Summation proves (1). If p lies
on the boundary of T, approximate it by points of int B, which exist
because B is full-dimensional, and pass to the finite affine sum.
In particular |B|/|T|>=min_i f_i. The stronger support constraint (1)
retains the actual position of B rather than assuming its centroid
coincides with that of T.

## 2. An exact planar bound from all three actual edge intervals

Let d=2. Suppose prescribed numbers a_i in (0,1], i=1,2,3, satisfy
f_i>=a_i. Then

    |B|/|T| >= 1-max_(i!=j)(1-a_i)(1-a_j).           (2)

This is the exact minimum under these edge-length lower bounds. If
a_(1)<=a_(2)<=a_(3) are the ordered values, (2) is

    |B|/|T| >= a_(1)+a_(2)-a_(1)*a_(2).             (3)

Proof. An invertible affine map reduces to any chosen triangle without
altering either area ratios or relative lengths on a fixed edge. Each
F_i is a nonempty closed interval on its edge. Their convex hull P is
contained in B. The part of T outside P consists, up to area-zero
boundaries, of the three corner triangles joining an original vertex
to the closest endpoints of the two adjacent intervals. This follows
also by walking around the six interval endpoints in cyclic boundary
order: their convex hull joins consecutive endpoints either along an
original edge or by precisely one such corner chord. Degenerate chords
or repeated endpoints cause no area contribution.

Label the edges 12,23,31. Write x_12,x_21 for their two normalized
endpoint gaps at vertices 1 and 2; define the other four similarly.
These numbers are nonnegative and satisfy

    x_12+x_21 <= r_12,
    x_23+x_32 <= r_23,
    x_31+x_13 <= r_31,        r_ij=1-a_ij.

The relative area removed at a vertex is the product of its two
incident normalized gaps. Thus

    1-|P|/|T| = x_12*x_13+x_21*x_23+x_31*x_32.      (4)

Increasing any gap cannot decrease this expression. Consequently its
maximum subject to the displayed upper budgets occurs with each edge
budget filled; such an increase is used only for an upper bound and
need not remain the actual interval configuration of a body. Substitute

    x_12=x, x_21=r_12-x,
    x_23=y, x_32=r_23-y,
    x_31=z, x_13=r_31-z.

Expression (4) becomes

    F(x,y,z)=x*(r_31-z)+(r_12-x)*y+z*(r_23-y).       (5)

It is affine separately in x,y,z on the rectangular box
[0,r_12] times [0,r_23] times [0,r_31]. Successively maximizing each
coordinate at an endpoint shows that its maximum is attained at a
box vertex. The eight vertex values are zero or one of
r_12*r_23, r_23*r_31, r_31*r_12. Therefore (4) is at most the largest
such product. Since B contains P, (2) follows.

For sharpness, choose the vertex joining the two edges i,j on which
(1-a_i)(1-a_j) is largest. Cut off that corner by the segment whose
two endpoint distances from the vertex are fractions 1-a_i and 1-a_j
of the incident edge lengths. Keep the closed complementary part of
T. The two retained incident-edge fractions are a_i,a_j, and the third
edge is retained in full. Its relative area is exactly the right-hand
side of (2). If either gap is zero, the largest product is zero only
when at most one gap is nonzero; then B=T realizes the value one and
satisfies all lower bounds. The positive a_i ensure the constructed
nontrivial truncation has positive area. This proves the claimed exact
optimization, not merely an asymptotic bound.

## 3. Consequence for normalized all-zero endpoint critical circuits

Assume the actual three-fiber hypotheses and full-rank minimal positive
continuous circuit of the companion note, with all B captures zero.
Use its allowed shear and positive normal scalings to write the caps
as v_i.x>=z and T={v_i.x<=1}; B is contained in this common simplex.
For every proper A cut set

    a_i=H_(d-1)(A intersect {v_i.x=-1})
                         /H_(d-1)(T intersect {v_i.x=1}).

The actual one-sided tilt condition proves f_i>=a_i>0. In particular
a_i<=1. In every dimension, (1) therefore gives

    |B|/|T| >= sum_(proper i) a_i lambda_i(p)

for every p in B, with zero lower bounds used at other indices.
For d=2, if all three A cuts are proper, the sharper exact planar
constraint (2) gives

    |B|/|T| >= a_(1)+a_(2)-a_(1)*a_(2).             (6)

Thus an independent assignment of three small endpoint volumes and
large supporting-facet capacities can fail actual convex realizability.
One tiny proper-section ratio is insufficient by itself to evade (6):
the second-smallest ratio also enters. The normalization of section
areas is per facet and is preserved by arbitrary invertible continuous
affine coordinates, since both compared parallel sections acquire the
same (d-1)-Jacobian. There is no transformation of the integer lattice.

Nothing here proves a lower bound on the mixed critical cap mass Q.
In particular the controlling simplex T need not be a minimum-volume
enclosing simplex, and zero in B is not assumed. Saturated opposite
cuts cannot be assigned positive a_i by this argument.
